title: Saubhari and the fish
hook: after years of austerity under the river, a sage watches a fish with its family, and an old desire wakes
carry: desire has no beginning, but it can end

segments.voice: Yesterday: King Nriga's cow. Good and bad both bind; offer the act.
screen: `GOOD AND BAD BOTH BIND; OFFER THE ACT.`

segments.voice: In the Bhagavata Purana, the sage Saubhari spends years in austerity under the waters of the Yamuna, still as a stone. One day he watches a king of fish playing in the river with its mates and its little ones. Something stirs in the sage, a wish he thought was long gone: a family, a home, a life like that. So he climbs out and goes to King Mandhata, who has fifty daughters, and asks for one.
screen: `YEARS UNDER THE RIVER.` → `A FISH AND ITS FAMILY.` → `AN OLD WISH WAKES.`

segments.voice: The king looks at this thin old ascetic and stalls: my daughters choose for themselves. So Saubhari uses his yogic power to make himself young and handsome, and all fifty choose him. He builds them palaces and lives a life of every pleasure, and it never feels like enough. At last he sees it. A whole life of tapas, he says, and I fell because I kept company with a fish. One sight had woken a desire that was waiting all along. He gives it up, goes back to the forest, and the story says he found freedom. Patanjali gives the reason in two sutras. 4.10: the traces of desire, vasanas, have no beginning, because the wish to go on living is everlasting. You can't find the first craving; there isn't one. That's the Hindu teaching of samsara: the round of births has no starting point. But 4.11 turns the key. The traces are held up by four supports: a cause, a result, a place in the mind to rest, and an object to lean on. Take the supports away, and the traces go. Saubhari's object was a happy fish. His own advice afterward, in the Bhagavata: if you want freedom, stay out of company lost in pleasure, and keep company with great souls. Hindus call that satsang, the company of the good. It's why families sing bhajans together and sit with the wise. Not because the past can be erased, but because what you feed grows. So: no beginning, and still, an end.
screen: `FIFTY PALACES. NEVER ENOUGH.` · `I FELL BECAUSE OF A FISH.` · `4.10: NO FIRST CRAVING.` · `4.11: TAKE AWAY THE SUPPORTS.` · `SATSANG: THE COMPANY OF THE GOOD.` · then, large: `DESIRE HAS NO BEGINNING, BUT IT CAN END.`

segments.voice: Let a small want come up on its own: to check the phone, to shift, to get up. Don't ask where it started; ask what it's leaning on right now, a thought, a sound, an itch, and name it quietly. Then, if you pray, end with a few lines of a bhajan or a name of God you love: good company for the mind. If you don't, end with one line you trust.
Vasana, the trace desire leaves behind, like a scent left in cloth. These traces have no first moment, because the will to live has none, but they rest on supports, and without them they fall away.
Your line: desire has no beginning, but it can end. Choose what you feed, and the company you keep. A week, done.

howItsDone: Hindus speak of vasanas and samskaras carried from life to life in a samsara without beginning, and value satsang, the company of the good, in bhajan singing, temple gatherings and time with the wise; the Yoga Sutras teach removing what supports the traces rather than hunting for their origin.

chat.meaning: Saubhari's old desire woke after years of tapas at the sight of a fish. Patanjali says the traces have no beginning, but without their supports they fall away: samsara has no first life, and it can end.
